newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Animal rights protesters back EU anti-test ban.
newsitem.headline: Animal rights protesters back EU anti-test ban.

text.p: Animal welfare protestors presented the European Commission with a petition on Wednesday carrying four million signatures and calling for a Europe-wide ban on cosmetics tested on animals.
An official from the cabinet of Consumer Affairs Commissioner Emma Bonino took the petition after President Jacques Santer, to whom it was addressed, refused to accept it.
Body Shop co-founder Anita Roddick, rock star Chrissie Hynde and British TV actor Andrew Sachs were among celebrities who presented the petition after a lengthy campaign.

"Three years ago it was agreed that from January 1, 1998 a Europe-wide ban would be imposed on the sale of cosmetics that had been tested on animals," said Roddick, whose cosmetics retail chain declares itself "Against Animal Testing".
"Now we know that the Commission is breaking that promise. This is a huge slap in the face for the four million Europeans who signed this petition," she added.
The Commission agreed the ban in 1993 conditional on finding suitable alternative testing methods by 1998 to make cosmetics safe for humans.

Roddick and other anti-testing campaigners say adequate alternatives to animal testing exist but fear they will not be enough to convince the Commission to give the go-ahead for the conditional ban in just over a year.
"All the Commission plans now is a review of its position in the year 2000," said Roddick.
Rory Macmillan, communications and information manager for the European Cosmetic, Toiletry and Perfumery Association (COLIPA), denied the Commission was backtracking on any promises.

"The Commission is not reneging on a ban. There was a possibility of a ban with regard to (product) ingredients based on the idea that alternatives would be agreed by the Organisation for Cooperation and Development," Macmillan said.

"It's clear that our industry is not in a position to stop all animal testing because alternative methods have not been evaluated. Therefore the Commission proposals to delay the ban are based on the state of science," he said by telephone.
COLIPA said in a statement that less than 0.03 per cent of animal tests in Europe were connected to cosmetics production.
